title: Dueling COVID-19 misinformation: Perceptions and behavior of the rural population from South Asian countries
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 399 rural adults in Bangladesh, India and Pakistan (2022) with an adapted Pew item on how much made-up news and information about coronavirus is around the respondent. The share perceiving any is reported (92.98%), as is the top-category share overall (42.11%) and per country. Perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment counts as RECALL.

estimates.date: April to June 2022 (India); May to June 2022 (Bangladesh and Pakistan); the Pakistan section elsewhere says June-July 2022; the abstract says 'early 2022'
estimates.measure_type: % of rural respondents who perceive that made-up news and information about the basic facts of the coronavirus is around them, to any degree
estimates.value_raw: 92.98% of the participants perceived the presence of COVID-19 misinformation to varying degrees around them
estimates.denominator: 399 rural adults from Bangladesh (n = 49), India (n = 300) and Pakistan (n = 50), convenience sample
estimates.definition: Answered anything other than the lowest/none category to QD, 'How much do you think made-up news and information about the basic facts of the coronavirus is around you?' (a great deal / a moderate amount / a little).
estimates.misinfo_def: The terms misinformation, disinformation, and fake news are explained as, "information that is false but not created with the intention of causing harm," and "information that is based on reality, used to inflict harm on a person, social group, organization or country" and "false stories that appear to be news, spread on the internet or using other media, usually created to influence political views or as a joke" respectively (UNESCO, 2018).
estimates.source_quote: Results indicate that 92.98% of the participants perceived the presence of COVID-19 misinformation to varying degrees around them with less than 10% finding it easy to verify the accuracy of the information.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; underlying item is QD, Figure 2, p. 768-769
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own perception; no external verification. Questionnaire adapted from a Pew Research Center (2021) survey, translated into Bengali, Hindi and Urdu; because of low rural literacy, data collectors read the questions aloud, explained where necessary and recorded the answers, so responses are interviewer-mediated.
estimates.moderator_quote: The convenience sampling method was applied to choose both the representative sample area and respondents.
estimates.notes: The 92.98% appears only in the abstract; the body gives the category shares (42.11% a great deal, 41.60% a moderate amount, 6.77% a little), which sum to 90.48%, not 92.98%. The figure is nonetheless stated verbatim, so it is kept under R8, but the discrepancy is unexplained and Figure 2 (which holds the full distribution) is not readable in the text file. Sample is a convenience sample of rural respondents in a few districts, not nationally representative, and is 68% female and 74% Hindu overall.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted (excluded by the protocol): QE, 'most participants, 94.24%, initially believed made-up news and information to be true before realizing it was fake'. This is belief in false claims, an explicit exclusion, even though the stem presupposes exposure. Note also that the country detail for QE contradicts the pooled figure ('in India, all participants were able to correctly identify made-up news, whereas 76% of participants from Pakistan were able to recognize false information' - which cannot coexist with 94.24% overall having been fooled). 2) NOT extracted: QG, the verification-difficulty distribution (9.02% easy, 7.02% very easy, 39.60%/42.61%/1.75% degrees of difficulty). This is perceived ability to verify information, not exposure to or prevalence of misinformation. 3) NOT extracted: QA self-perceived knowledge of coronavirus, QB mask wearing, QC vaccination status - not misinformation measures. 4) NOT extracted: the sentiment-analysis emotion distribution from open-ended Q-F (no percentages given in the text; reported only as a histogram). 5) NOT extracted: figures the paper cites from elsewhere - 'out of 112 million posts about COVID-19 on social media, 40% contained information from unreliable sources (FBK)' and 'one out of six COVID-19 information generated in 2020 was fake' in India (Kanozia et al.), both barred by R8. 6) Judgement call: I split by country because the paper reports QD separately for each, but the country figures use inconsistent category labels ('a lot' vs 'a great deal') and do not reconcile with the pooled 42.11%. An adjudicator may prefer to keep only the two Multi-country rows. 7) Sample sizes: the abstract says 400 respondents, the results tables say N = 399. I used 399 throughout.

rob.design: Cross-sectional, interviewer-administered paper survey of a convenience sample of 399 rural adults in Bangladesh (n = 49, five villages in Mohanpur upazila, Rajshahi), India (n = 300, rural Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan) and Pakistan (n = 50, rural Punjab), fielded April-June 2022 (Pakistan reported as May-June and elsewhere June-July 2022). Sample size allocated by country population, not by design power; no sampling frame, no response rate reported, no refusal count. Data collectors were local graduate students and a local researcher who read the questions aloud and recorded answers because of low rural literacy, which introduces interviewer effects. Instrument: 12 items (7 on COVID-19 misinformation, 5 demographic) adapted from a Pew Research Center (2021) survey, translated into Bengali, Hindi and Urdu; no pilot, reliability or validity statistics reported for the adapted instrument. Analysis: descriptive shares plus Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests for demographic differences; sentiment analysis of one open-ended item with the R syuzhet package. Sample is skewed (67.92% female, 74.19% Hindu, 48.62% aged 35-50) and religion is almost perfectly confounded with country. Internal inconsistencies in the reported percentages (see notes and missed_or_uncertain) are a further concern.
